items.followUp: Define a heteroatomic molecule and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must state that a homoatomic molecule contains atoms of the same element.
rubric.description: Defines a homoatomic molecule as one made of atoms of the same element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that its atoms are of the same kind or element.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as H₂ or O₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any valid homoatomic molecule.

modelAnswer: A homoatomic molecule is a molecule made up of atoms of the same element.

items.followUp: State the main idea of the Law of Octaves and name its proposer.

rubric.why: Newlands used increasing atomic mass as the order of arrangement.
rubric.description: States that Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increasing atomic mass order.

rubric.why: The similarity of every eighth element is the defining observation in Newlands’ arrangement.
rubric.description: States that every eighth element had properties similar to the first.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the every-eighth similarity.

modelAnswer: Newlands arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic masses.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element were similar to those of the first, like notes in a musical octave.

items.followUp: Name the elements in the second period of the periodic table.

rubric.why: Hydrogen is one of the two elements in the first period.
Helium is the other element in the first period.

modelAnswer: The first period also contains helium (He).

items.followUp: Define ionization energy and give one example of its use in describing an atom.

rubric.why: Electron affinity refers to energy released when an atom gains an electron.
rubric.description: Defines electron affinity as energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the energy-release definition involving acceptance of an electron.

rubric.why: The example should show an atom accepting an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as chlorine gaining an electron to form Cl⁻.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example or reaction.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) + energy.

items.followUp: What causes a bond between two different atoms to be polar?

rubric.why: A difference in electronegativity causes unequal attraction for the shared electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies a difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the atoms have different electronegativities.

rubric.why: Unequal sharing creates partial charges and makes the covalent bond polar.
rubric.description: Explains that unequal sharing of the electron pair produces polarity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for unequal sharing or the resulting partial charges.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond becomes polar when the bonded atoms have different electronegativities.
The more electronegative atom attracts the shared electron pair more strongly, so the electrons are shared unequally and partial charges develop.

items.followUp: State two conditions that favour the formation of an ionic bond.

rubric.why: Atoms need available valence electrons to share in forming a covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that the atoms have unpaired valence electrons available for sharing.

rubric.why: A small electronegativity difference favours sharing rather than complete electron transfer.
rubric.description: States that the atoms have a small or zero electronegativity difference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this condition, or for another valid textbook condition for covalent-bond formation.

modelAnswer: The atoms should have unpaired electrons in their valence shells that can be shared.
The electronegativity difference between the atoms should be small (or zero), so the shared electrons are attracted by both atoms.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a shared pair and an unshared pair of electrons?

rubric.why: A lone pair is not shared between atoms in a covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not shared in bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for distinguishing a lone pair as unshared.

rubric.why: A bond pair is the electron pair shared between atoms to form a covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that a bond pair is shared between atoms and forms a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for distinguishing a bond pair as shared.

modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons belonging to one atom that is not shared in a covalent bond.
A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and give two allotropes of oxygen.

rubric.why: Allotropy describes an element existing in more than one form in the same physical state.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy as the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition; the same physical state may be stated or implied.

rubric.why: The examples must be different forms of the same element.
rubric.description: Gives correct examples, such as diamond and graphite (carbon) or oxygen and ozone.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct pair of allotropes.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the property of an element to exist in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
For example, carbon exists as diamond and graphite; oxygen exists as O₂ and O₃.
